scenes.heading: Message Queues
scenes.narration: A message queue buffers work between producers and consumers, decoupling them and smoothing out load spikes.

scenes.heading: What queues give you
bullets: Buffering so producers outpace slow consumers.
scenes.narration: A queue absorbs bursts, letting fast producers hand off work that slower consumers drain over time. Sender and receiver never talk directly, so either can go down without losing messages. Acknowledgements ensure a message is redelivered if processing fails, and multiple consumers can pull from the same queue to scale throughput.

scenes.heading: Message lifecycle
scenes.narration: A producer places a message on the queue, and the broker stores it durably until someone is ready. A consumer pulls the message and processes it, but the message is not truly gone yet. Only after the consumer sends an acknowledgement does the broker remove it, guaranteeing at-least-once delivery.

scenes.heading: Queue vs pub-sub
scenes.narration: A point-to-point queue delivers each message to exactly one consumer, which is ideal for distributing tasks among workers. Publish-subscribe broadcasts each message to all subscribers, which suits announcing events to many interested systems. The pattern you pick depends on whether work is shared or shared out.

scenes.text: Message queues buffer and decouple producers from consumers, using acknowledgements for reliable delivery and competing consumers for scale.
scenes.narration: By absorbing spikes and confirming delivery, a queue keeps systems responsive and resilient even when one side falls behind.
